title: Padres Face Tough NLDS Roster Choices: 12 Pitchers, 3 Catchers Up for Selection
body:
SAN DIEGO – After a flawless performance in the Wild Card Series, the San Diego Padres now face a roster conundrum as they prepare for the National League Division Series. The club’s 12‑pitcher, three‑catcher configuration that helped sweep the Chicago Cubs will be put to the test when the coaching staff must trim the squad to the 26‑player limit for the NLDS, forcing tough choices among relievers, starters and the catching corps.

The Padres entered the postseason with a flexible, depth‑first approach that paid dividends in the best‑of‑three series. Manager Mike Shildt’s decision to carry an extra arm in the bullpen allowed him to ride a variety of relievers without overtaxing any single arm. The team’s five‑man rotation—featuring the likes of Blake Snell, Yu Darvish, and the emergent youngster Joe Kelly—delivered quality starts in each game, while the bullpen’s collective ERA of 2.31 kept the Cubs at bay. Even the seldom‑used Game 3 starter candidates, who never saw the mound because the series ended in two games, were kept ready, underscoring the depth Shildt cultivated.

Now that the Padres must reduce their roster, the biggest question revolves around the twelve pitchers currently on the bench. The club’s front office has already indicated that the two most vulnerable arms—reliever Jhoan Duran, who struggled with command in Game 2, and left‑handed specialist Luke Weaver, whose recent outings have been marked by high walk rates—are likely candidates for removal. Conversely, the hot‑handed closer Josh Hader, who notched a save in Game 1 and has been dominant all season, is a lock to stay. The real dilemma lies with the middle‑relief corps: who will fill the void left by Duran and Weaver? Veteran right‑hander Adam Cimber, who has been effective against left‑handed hitters, and rookie prospect Nick Lodolo, who showed promise in limited action, are both under consideration.

The catching group presents a similarly thorny issue. San Diego entered the postseason with three catchers—Luis Campusano, Austin Hedges and rookie J.T. Realmuto (who was called up from Triple‑A after an injury to the starter). Campusano’s strong defensive work and respectable bat (a .260 average with two RBIs in the series) make him a near‑certainty for the roster. Hedges, a defensive specialist, offers a left‑handed bat and veteran presence, but his offensive numbers have been modest all year. Realmuto, though untested at the major‑league level, brings a high ceiling and a left‑handed bat that could be valuable in a matchup‑heavy NLDS. The coaching staff must decide whether to retain three catchers for flexibility or trim down to two to free a spot for an additional pitcher or bench player.

Beyond the immediate personnel decisions, the Padres’ strategic outlook for the NLDS hinges on the matchup against the Los Angeles Dodgers. San Diego’s rotation, while deep, will be forced to start a different pitcher in Game 1 than originally planned, as Snell is slated to rest after logging 13 innings in the Wild Card Series. Darvish, who has been a workhorse all season, is expected to take the mound, but his recent left‑handed splits against the Dodgers’ lineup have been less convincing. This may prompt Shildt to consider a bullpen game in the opening contest, leveraging the depth of his relievers to neutralize the Dodgers’ potent offense.

In the days ahead, the Padres will convene to finalize their NLDS roster, balancing the desire to preserve the depth that served them so well in Chicago with the constraints of a 26‑player limit. The decisions made now will not only shape the immediate series but also set a precedent for how the organization values versatility versus specialization in postseason play. As the Padres look to build on their Wild Card triumph, the roster cuts will be a litmus test for a club that has embraced depth as a competitive advantage—one that could prove decisive as they chase a first World Series title since 1998.
